network.overall_strategy: A connected, target-focused network with 27 molecule nodes, 20 reaction nodes, and 10 distinct reaction sequences. The pathways comprise three alternative photoredox implementations of lactaldehyde/Strecker chemistry, aminomalononitrile chemistry, glycine-fed and oligoglycine-fed chemistry, bulk HCN chemistry, cyanide radiolysis, and two discharge configurations. These are not ten independently validated elementary mechanisms: implementation variants, unresolved reaction ensembles, and speculative environmental extensions are identified explicitly. L-threonine is the target node, but no route establishes biological stereoselectivity; D-threonine and, where supported or mechanistically expected, allothreonine are separate products. Historical reports lacking enantiomer-resolved measurements are represented by an expected racemic threonine pair, not a claimed measured ratio. All modeled environments are terrestrial Surface settings, without molecular oxygen or enzymes. Cryogenic extraterrestrial experiments are excluded rather than relabeled as terrestrial surface chemistry. Photochemistry occurs in illuminated water, whereas subsequent accumulation and hydrolysis require shielded or temporally separated conditions. Strong laboratory hydrolysis is not treated as demonstrated environmental hydrolysis. Unresolved polymer, radiation, and discharge pathways are explicitly multistage ensemble nodes; fictitious molecular identities are not assigned to their heterogeneous residues. Some ensemble coproducts provide explicitly provisional atom-balance closure rather than experimentally resolved product distributions. Terminal coproducts use the schema's intermediate role because no coproduct role is available.

reactions.name: Acetaldehyde cyanohydrin formation

conditions.other: Approximately neutral to mildly alkaline water; cyanide speciation controls reaction rate. Retain volatile HCN and acetaldehyde in a locally concentrated reservoir.

reactions.mechanism: Reversible cyanide addition to the aldehyde carbonyl followed by proton transfer produces racemic lactonitrile.
reactions.reasoning: This is the defined acetaldehyde-entry step of the threonine-precursor sequence reported by Ritson and Sutherland (2013). No mineral is required. Concentration, volatilization, and competing cyanide reactions limit environmental flux; cyanide storage in closed-basin settings has independent geochemical support from Toner and Catling (2019).

reactions.name: Cu(I)-assisted sulfidic photoreduction of lactonitrile

conditions.other: Anoxic, UV-transparent shallow water near pH 7; laboratory reference uses 254 nm irradiation. Representative related-module conditions were 10 mM nitrile, 30 mM H2S, 33 mM phosphate, and 10 mol% CuCN, not a universal recipe for every substrate.

reactions.mechanism: Photogenerated reducing equivalents reduce the nitrile to an imine-level intermediate; hydrolysis releases lactaldehyde and ammonia. Sulfide supplies reducing equivalents.
reactions.reasoning: Ritson and Sutherland (2013) obtained lactaldehyde in 19% yield after two hours in the acetaldehyde-cyanohydrin photochemical system. This supports the carbon transformation, not identical yields under all modeled conditions. Elemental sulfur is an oxidized-sulfur endmember for net redox bookkeeping; actual sulfur products may include polysulfides. Cu/Fe sulfide precipitation and sulfur-associated UV attenuation constrain deployment (Ranjan et al., 2018).

reactions.name: Copper-free sulfidic photoreduction candidate

conditions.other: Anoxic UV irradiation with H2S/HS- near neutral pH; no added copper. Target-substrate irradiation time and effective concentrations are unestablished.

reactions.mechanism: Sulfide-derived photochemistry supplies reducing equivalents for nitrile reduction and subsequent imine hydrolysis without an added copper mediator.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative threonine-specific extension. Patel et al. (2015) support copper-independent reduction within H2S-containing cyanosulfidic chemistry, but the supplied evidence does not establish a separate copper-free lactonitrile-to-lactaldehyde yield. This is an alternative photoredox implementation, not an independently demonstrated threonine synthesis. Sulfur availability and UV compatibility remain constrained (Ranjan et al., 2018). S8 is provisional redox-endmember bookkeeping.

reactions.name: Ferrocyanide-sulfite photoreduction candidate
agents: Dissolved hexacyanidoferrate(II), ferrocyanide, as photoredox mediator

conditions.other: Anoxic UV-exposed water containing sulfite/bisulfite; approximately neutral to mildly alkaline candidate conditions. Lactonitrile-specific optimization is not established.

reactions.mechanism: Photoinduced electron-transfer chemistry reduces the nitrile; imine hydrolysis gives lactaldehyde and ammonia. Sulfite supplies reducing equivalents.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative substrate-specific extension of experimentally demonstrated HCN reductive homologation using sulfite and ferrocyanide (Xu et al., 2018). That study did not establish a new threonine endpoint or the lactonitrile conversion modeled here. Sulfite provides a chemically motivated alternative where sustained hydrosulfide is difficult (Ranjan et al., 2018). Sulfate is a possible oxidized-sulfur balance endmember, not an assertion that it is the unique measured photoproduct.

reactions.name: Lactaldehyde cyanohydrin formation

conditions.other: Near-neutral aqueous cyanide; protect the accumulating hydroxyaldehyde-derived pool from excessive continued irradiation and competing condensation.

reactions.mechanism: Reversible cyanide addition to lactaldehyde produces 2,3-dihydroxybutanenitrile as a stereoisomeric cyanohydrin pool.
reactions.reasoning: Ritson and Sutherland (2013) describe conversion of lactaldehyde through its cyanohydrin into the threonine/allothreonine aminonitrile. Explicitly retaining this node avoids conflating aldehyde capture with amination or nitrile hydrolysis. Environmental lactaldehyde persistence remains an unmeasured bottleneck.

reactions.name: Strecker aminonitrile formation from the lactaldehyde cyanohydrin pool

conditions.other: Excess ammonia with retained cyanide; days-to-weeks residence may be necessary. pH must permit both carbonyl/iminium chemistry and sufficient available ammonia.

reactions.mechanism: Cyanohydrin dissociation regenerates lactaldehyde and cyanide; ammonia-derived imine/iminium formation and cyanide capture yield the aminonitrile. This is not assumed to be direct displacement of hydroxide from the cyanohydrin.
reactions.reasoning: The threonine/allothreonine Strecker aminonitrile is an experimentally supported endpoint of Ritson and Sutherland (2013). Related conversions took days to weeks. Competing carbonyl reactions, ammonia loss, and cyanohydrin equilibria therefore matter; the transformation should not be represented as instantaneous.

reactions.name: Threonine-family aminonitrile hydrolysis
agents: Hydronium ions for specific acid catalysis

conditions.other: Candidate acidic pool, approximately pH 1-3, after transfer or temporal acidification of the aminonitrile-containing water. Required residence time and competing decomposition rates are unknown.

reactions.mechanism: Sequential nitrile hydration through an amide and subsequent amide hydrolysis form the carboxylic acid and release ammonia, predominantly ammonium at the stated pH.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative environmental completion of an experimentally established precursor route. Ritson and Sutherland (2013) demonstrated the aminonitrile, not a quantified free-threonine yield under these proposed pool conditions. The chemistry is standard nitrile hydrolysis, but its useful environmental rate is a major unresolved bottleneck. The listed stereoisomers are possible products, not equal-yield coefficients or a demonstrated L-selective outcome.

reactions.name: HCN oligomerization to aminomalononitrile

conditions.other: Concentrated HCN/cyanide in mildly alkaline water, approximately pH 8-10. The node represents trimer formation within competing oligomerization, not quantitative conversion into a pure trimer.

reactions.mechanism: Successive cyanide/HCN addition and proton-transfer reactions generate the HCN trimer aminomalononitrile.
reactions.reasoning: Aminomalononitrile is the established HCN trimer used in Thanassi's threonine chemistry (Thanassi, 1975); broader ammonium-cyanide oligomerization is supported by Lowe et al. (1963). Selective accumulation and retention of the trimer under the proposed environmental conditions are not established. Cyanide concentration is a substantive requirement rather than an assumed ocean-wide condition (Toner and Catling, 2019).

reactions.name: Aminomalononitrile C-C addition to acetaldehyde

conditions.other: Approximately neutral aqueous solution; preserve acetaldehyde and avoid excessive competing HCN oligomerization. No mineral catalyst is imposed.

reactions.mechanism: The activated central carbon of aminomalononitrile forms a C-C bond with acetaldehyde, giving a hydroxyethyl-substituted dinitrile skeleton.
reactions.reasoning: Thanassi (1975) demonstrated threonine and allothreonine after reaction of aminomalononitrile with acetaldehyde and subsequent hydrolysis/decarboxylation. Kuroda et al. (2020) describe the C-C-forming reaction as occurring under almost neutral aqueous conditions. The molecular adduct is a mechanistic representation of the required connectivity, not a claim of a separately measured isolated-intermediate yield.

reactions.name: Hydrolysis of the substituted aminomalononitrile

conditions.other: Proposed acidic pool, approximately pH 1-3, with prolonged residence. This is not assumed equivalent in rate or yield to the laboratory acid-hydrolysis procedure.

reactions.mechanism: Hydrolysis of both nitrile groups, through amide intermediates, generates a substituted aminomalonic acid and releases ammonia.
reactions.reasoning: The combined acid-hydrolysis/decarboxylation endpoint is experimentally supported by Thanassi (1975) and discussed by Kuroda et al. (2020). The discrete diacid is a mechanistically inferred intermediate; its accumulation was not established in the supplied findings. Completion at the proposed milder environmental acidity is speculative and may be too slow or unselective.

reactions.name: Decarboxylation of the hydroxyethyl-substituted aminomalonic acid

conditions.other: Acidic hydrolysis pool; decarboxylation may overlap with preceding hydrolysis rather than occur after isolation of the diacid.

reactions.mechanism: Loss of one carboxyl group as CO2 and protonation of the resulting carbon center produce the threonine and allothreonine skeletons.
reactions.reasoning: Hydrolysis followed by decarboxylation accounts for the experimentally reported D,L-threonine and allothreonine products (Thanassi, 1975; Kuroda et al., 2020). Standalone kinetics for this inferred intermediate under the modeled pool conditions are not supplied. Neither enantioselectivity nor a quantitative threonine:allothreonine ratio is assumed.

reactions.name: Formaldehyde Strecker supply of aminoacetonitrile

conditions.other: Near-neutral to mildly alkaline concentrated water containing formaldehyde, ammonia, and cyanide; retain volatile feedstocks.

reactions.mechanism: Formaldehyde forms an imine/iminium species with ammonia; cyanide addition gives aminoacetonitrile.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative upstream network integration relative to the supplied research, which does not separately document this glycine-supply experiment. The transformation is established general Strecker chemistry and is chemically analogous to the experimentally supported hydroxyaldehyde Strecker module of Ritson and Sutherland (2013). It supplies glycine without invoking the unsupported claim that generic aldehyde/ammonia mixtures directly yield threonine; Koga and Naraoka (2017) provide a negative constraint on that latter claim.

reactions.name: Aminoacetonitrile hydrolysis to glycine
agents: Hydronium ions for specific acid catalysis

conditions.other: Acidified water, approximately pH 1-3; environmental hydrolysis time is unspecified. Subsequent adjustment toward pH 3.3-3.7 enables the aldehyde/glycine stage.

reactions.mechanism: Nitrile hydration and amide hydrolysis yield glycine and ammonia/ammonium.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative environmental supply module relative to the supplied studies. General aminonitrile hydrolysis supports the chemistry, but the cited threonine research does not establish this step's rate in the modeled pool. Its purpose is to provide the glycine substrate actually used by Ivanov and Ivanov (1983), while keeping the nitrile-hydrolysis bottleneck explicit.

reactions.name: Glycine-acetaldehyde threonine-forming reaction ensemble

conditions.other: pH 3.3-3.7; homogeneous solution without inorganic solids. Requires sufficient glycine and acetaldehyde concentration and residence time.

reactions.mechanism: Net C-C bond formation between the glycine alpha carbon and acetaldehyde gives the beta-hydroxy amino-acid skeleton. An imine-mediated aldol-like description is plausible, but the experimentally observed reaction network is not mechanistically resolved.
reactions.reasoning: Ivanov and Ivanov (1983) reported threonine among products of glycine/oligoglycine and aldehyde chemistry at these temperatures and pH, without inorganic solids. This supports a threonine-producing reaction ensemble, not a selective elementary aldol reaction. The supplied findings provide no isolated yield or stereoisomer ratio; the two listed threonine enantiomers express the achiral-model expectation, and omission of allo products here does not imply their absence.

reactions.name: Carbonyl-sulfide-mediated glycylglycine supply

conditions.other: Mildly alkaline water, approximately pH 8-9, locally supplied with volcanic carbonyl sulfide. COS is a consumed activating reagent, not a catalyst. Later acidification is required for the aldehyde stage.

reactions.mechanism: COS activates glycine through thiocarbamate/N-carboxyanhydride chemistry; attack by another glycine forms glycylglycine, with net release of CO2 and H2S.
reactions.reasoning: This supply step is outside the provided threonine bibliography. COS-mediated prebiotic peptide formation is experimentally supported by Leman, Orgel and Ghadiri (2004), while its coupling to the present threonine network is speculative. It is included to supply a defined oligoglycine substrate rather than assume a pre-existing peptide. COS hydrolysis competes with activation, and no productive yield for this complete staged pathway is established.

reactions.name: Oligoglycine-acetaldehyde chemistry with hydrolytic threonine release
agents: Hydronium ions during the peptide-cleavage stage

conditions.temperature: 333-353 K for aldehyde exposure; proposed cleavage up to 370 K
conditions.catalyst: Hydronium ions for hydrolytic cleavage only
conditions.other: Aldehyde exposure at pH 3.3-3.7 without inorganic solids. Release from residual peptide-bound material may require later stronger acidity or longer residence; its environmental rate is unresolved.

reactions.mechanism: A lumped peptide-fed ensemble combines hydroxyethyl incorporation and peptide cleavage. The represented net branch converts one glycine residue into threonine while releasing another as glycine; functionalization before versus after cleavage is unresolved.
reactions.reasoning: Ivanov and Ivanov (1983) included oligoglycine substrates and detected threonine in their product inventory. The supplied evidence does not prove a unique intact-glycylglycine C-C-forming mechanism or distinguish it from chemistry following partial peptide hydrolysis. Consequently this defined peptide-fed sequence is a speculative mechanistic specialization of a supported reaction ensemble, not a proven independent elementary threonine pathway.

reactions.name: Bulk HCN-ammonia chemistry followed by hydrolysis: unresolved ensemble
agents: Hydronium ions during the subsequent hydrolysis stage

conditions.temperature: 300-350 K for oligomer formation; proposed environmental hydrolysis at 350-370 K
conditions.other: Concentrated alkaline/ammoniacal HCN first; subsequent acidic hydrolysis is a separate stage within this ensemble node. Historical analytical workups used strong acid, including approximately 6 M HCl near 373 K; a pH 1-3 natural replacement is unvalidated.

reactions.mechanism: HCN oligomerization and rearrangement produce heterogeneous nitrogen-rich material that releases threonine on hydrolysis. No particular aminonitrile, peptide, or polymer structure is assigned to the unresolved residue.
reactions.reasoning: Hydrolysate threonine is supported by Matthews and Moser (1966, 1967), with related ammonium-cyanide complexity demonstrated by Lowe et al. (1963). Free threonine before workup was not established. Environmental completion is speculative. CO2 and released ammonia provide a possible atom-balanced disproportionation/hydrolysis projection; the studies do not establish this unique coproduct balance. Ammonia occurs on both sides because it is present initially and may also be liberated.

reactions.name: Aqueous cyanide radiolysis followed by hydrolysis: unresolved ensemble
agents: Hydronium ions during the subsequent hydrolysis stage

conditions.temperature: 300-310 K for the modeled irradiation stage; proposed environmental hydrolysis at 350-370 K
conditions.catalyst: Hydronium ions during hydrolysis; no irradiation catalyst
conditions.other: Oxygen-free HCN solution; reported HCN concentrations were 0.004-0.1 M and the laboratory gamma dose rate was about 2 kGy per hour. Natural dose delivery and replacement of analytical strong-acid hydrolysis remain unresolved.

reactions.mechanism: Ionizing radiation initiates water-derived and cyanide-derived radical reactions, producing heterogeneous hydrolyzable oligomers. Subsequent hydrolysis releases threonine.
reactions.reasoning: Post-hydrolysis threonine was demonstrated by Sweeney, Toste and Ponnamperuma (1976) and independently supported by Draganić et al. (1977), who identified radical-initiated oligomer formation and approximately racemic products. A cobalt-60 source is a laboratory proxy, not an assumed Hadean resource. Environmental completion is speculative. CO2/ammonia are provisional atom-balance closure products, not an experimentally assigned complete radiation-product inventory.

reactions.name: H2S-rich wet electrical-discharge synthesis ensemble
agents: Tungsten electrode/sulfur interfaces in the laboratory apparatus; catalytic contribution unresolved

conditions.temperature: 300-370 K bulk water and gas; transient discharge channels are much hotter
conditions.other: Electrical discharge coupled to circulating water. Reported gas partial pressures were approximately 258 mmHg CH4, 100 mmHg H2S, 250 mmHg NH3, and 87 mmHg CO2. Applicable as a local or transient reducing scenario, not an assumed global atmosphere.

reactions.mechanism: An unresolved gas-phase radical and aqueous reaction network produces threonine-containing material. Carbonyls and nitriles are plausible intermediates, but no unique threonine-forming sequence is assigned.
reactions.reasoning: Parker et al. (2011) detected threonine in archived material from the H2S-rich Miller experiment. The evidence supports the overall product accessibility, not a resolved elementary mechanism or selective synthesis. Sulfur deposition near tungsten electrodes prevents describing the apparatus as rigorously surface-independent. H2 and elemental sulfur provide plausible net redox coproducts, without asserting a measured exclusive balance. The reducing gas composition is a substantial geochemical restriction.

reactions.name: Dry methane-ammonia discharge followed by residue hydrolysis
agents: Hydronium ions during the later aqueous hydrolysis stage

conditions.temperature: 300-370 K bulk gas during discharge; proposed environmental hydrolysis at 350-370 K
conditions.pressure: Approximately 1 atm in the modeled terrestrial scenario
conditions.other: The aqueous flag describes the initial dry CH4/NH3 discharge. Water is consumed only during a later aqueous workup explicitly included in this multistage node. Electrical channels are transiently hot. A natural acidic workup replacing laboratory hydrolysis has not been validated.

reactions.mechanism: Electrical processing of dry reducing gases forms heterogeneous nitrogenous residues; hydrolysis subsequently releases amino acids including threonine. Hydrogen is a plausible net dehydrogenation coproduct.
reactions.reasoning: Matthews and Moser (1966) reported threonine among amino acids released by hydrolysis of dry methane/ammonia discharge residues, as summarized in the supplied research. This configuration is distinct from the wet H2S-rich Miller apparatus, but its immediate threonine precursor remains unidentified. Environmental hydrolysis and useful natural gas compositions are speculative; the edge must not be interpreted as demonstrated gas-phase formation of free threonine.

pathways.name: Cu(I)-sulfide photoredox homologation and Strecker completion
pathways.description: Acetaldehyde and HCN form lactonitrile, which undergoes the best-supported threonine-specific photoreduction to lactaldehyde. Cyanohydrin and aminonitrile formation follow. Final free-amino-acid production remains conditional on effective environmental nitrile hydrolysis.

pathways.name: Copper-free sulfidic photoredox variant
pathways.description: Uses the same resolved carbon-skeleton sequence as P1 but substitutes a copper-free sulfide photoreduction candidate. This is a distinct implementation path, not a separately demonstrated complete threonine synthesis.

pathways.name: Ferrocyanide-sulfite photoredox variant
pathways.description: Substitutes sulfite and an Fe(II)-cyanide photoredox mediator for the sulfidic reduction module. The lactonitrile-specific application is speculative; downstream cyanohydrin and aminonitrile chemistry follows the supported Strecker branch.

pathways.name: HCN-trimer alkylation, hydrolysis, and decarboxylation
pathways.description: HCN supplies aminomalononitrile, which adds to acetaldehyde and then undergoes hydrolysis/decarboxylation. The laboratory threonine/allothreonine endpoint is demonstrated, but environmental trimer accumulation and sufficiently rapid natural hydrolysis remain unresolved.

pathways.name: Strecker-supplied glycine followed by acetaldehyde coupling
pathways.description: A proposed upstream formaldehyde Strecker module supplies glycine. The target-forming stage uses the experimentally reported catalyst-free glycine/acetaldehyde ensemble in warm, weakly acidic water. Neither selective threonine production nor a complete environmental yield is established.

pathways.name: COS-activated oligoglycine-fed pathway
pathways.description: Strecker-supplied glycine is activated with carbonyl sulfide to generate glycylglycine before aldehyde exposure and hydrolytic release. This differs from P5 by a chemically motivated peptide stage, but intact-peptide functionalization versus reaction after partial cleavage is unresolved.

pathways.name: Bulk HCN-ammonia hydrolysate pathway
pathways.description: Concentrated HCN/ammonia chemistry generates unresolved hydrolyzable material containing the threonine skeleton. The multistage ensemble includes hydrolysis explicitly. Laboratory hydrolysate detection is supported; environmental release of free threonine is conditional and the immediate molecular precursor is unknown.

pathways.name: Ionizing-radiation-initiated cyanide pathway
pathways.description: Aqueous cyanide radiolysis creates hydrolyzable oligomers that release threonine during workup. This energy-driven pathway is experimentally supported at the hydrolysate level, but natural dosimetry, residue identities, and environmental hydrolysis remain unresolved.

pathways.name: Wet H2S-rich discharge pathway
pathways.description: Electrical processing of methane, ammonia, carbon dioxide, hydrogen sulfide, and circulating water accesses threonine through an unresolved ensemble. The specific laboratory product detection is supported, while a unique mechanism and broadly representative early-Earth atmospheric composition are not.

pathways.name: Dry methane-ammonia discharge and hydrolysis pathway
pathways.description: Dry reducing-gas discharge generates nitrogenous residues that subsequently release threonine on hydrolysis. This is operationally distinct from P9 and explicitly workup-dependent; it does not establish free threonine in the initial dry reactor or a validated natural hydrolysis stage.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This is a chemically well-defined route with correctly identified intermediates. Ritson and Sutherland support lactaldehyde formation at 19% yield and subsequent threonine-family aminonitrile formation, rather than a demonstrated free-threonine endpoint. Treating cyanohydrin-to-aminonitrile conversion as chemistry of an equilibrating pool is appropriate. Shielding or temporal separation after photochemistry is physically sensible, but environmental hydrolysis kinetics, intermediate survival, and simultaneous availability of UV, sulfide and Cu(I) remain unspecified. Racemic production can include the L-threonine target without establishing enantiopurity.
suggestions: Attach reaction-specific references and specify substrate concentrations, pH, irradiation dose, Cu(I) loading and sulfide speciation for rxn_002.
Demonstrate rxn_007 under an explicitly defined surface-water regime, measuring hydrolysis against precursor and threonine degradation.
Represent stereoisomer yields independently of the integer coefficients used for balance closure.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Copper-free sulfidic photoreduction is a plausible implementation, and the supplied literature does not make copper universally indispensable. Nevertheless, support for copper-free reduction generally does not establish quantitative lactonitrile-to-lactaldehyde performance under this pathway's conditions. The network correctly labels rxn_003 as a candidate. Downstream Strecker chemistry is credible, but both the substrate-specific photoreduction and environmentally effective aminonitrile hydrolysis require validation.
suggestions: Measure lactaldehyde yield and competing products from lactonitrile under explicitly copper-free conditions.
Specify the sulfide concentration, UV spectrum, irradiation duration and optical depth rather than assuming performance transfers from another photoredox implementation.
Establish a compatible shielded hydrolysis stage with measured free-threonine recovery.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Xu et al. support sulfite/ferrocyanide-driven reductive homologation, but the supplied research does not demonstrate this specific lactonitrile-to-threonine sequence. The balanced sulfite-to-sulfate equation establishes conservation, not substrate selectivity or productive photoredox turnover. Ferrocyanide is identified in the reaction title, but its loading, speciation, availability and fate are not operationally specified. The downstream chemistry remains plausible, with the same environmental hydrolysis gap as P1.
suggestions: Provide lactonitrile-specific experimental evidence for rxn_004, including lactaldehyde yield and competing reduction products.
Record ferrocyanide and sulfite concentrations, pH, irradiation conditions and any catalyst replenishment requirements.
Validate free-threonine release under a defined environmental hydrolysis regime.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This is the strongest endpoint-supported pathway in the submitted network. Thanassi directly supports threonine and allothreonine production from aminomalononitrile/acetaldehyde chemistry after hydrolysis and decarboxylation. The proposed carbon connectivity and transformations are chemically coherent. However, rxn_008 represents access to an oligomerization product rather than selective conversion of HCN into a persistent aminomalononitrile pool. The mild conditions of the C-C-forming step should not be extended to the subsequent acid hydrolysis. The modeled hydrolyzed adduct is plausible but is not established here as an independently accumulated intermediate.
suggestions: Quantify aminomalononitrile formation, persistence and competition with other HCN oligomers under the proposed surface conditions.
Specify acid strength, temperature and residence time for hydrolysis/decarboxylation, distinguishing laboratory workup from environmental processing.
Identify mol_019 explicitly as a mechanistic intermediate unless its isolation or direct observation is documented.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Formaldehyde Strecker chemistry provides a credible glycine supply, and Ivanov and Ivanov support threonine formation from glycine/aldehyde mixtures at pH 3.3-3.7 and 60-80 C without inorganic solids. Describing rxn_014 as an ensemble is appropriate because the reported products were diverse. Its net equation must not imply selective or quantitative threonine formation. Glycine-supply hydrolysis still requires specified conditions, and the supplied evidence does not establish the complete product or stereoisomer distribution for the modeled feed.
suggestions: Encode the demonstrated warm, weakly acidic conditions and document the actual glycine and acetaldehyde concentrations and residence time.
Measure glycine-supply hydrolysis and threonine formation under compatible conditions, including competing reactions and product loss.
Treat allothreonine and other products as unresolved unless excluded analytically; do not infer their absence from omitted product nodes.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: COS-mediated peptide formation makes glycylglycine supply chemically credible, and the Ivanov study supports threonine-forming chemistry involving oligoglycine. However, the submission provides no reaction-specific support or operating conditions for the COS module. The supplied target literature also does not establish the exact glycylglycine-only conversion and product allocation represented by rxn_016. Compatibility among peptide formation, COS hydrolysis, aldehyde coupling and amino-acid release remains to be demonstrated. This is an evidence and condition-specification gap, not an objection to the chosen feedstock or number of stages.
suggestions: Cite and specify the COS-mediated glycylglycine conditions, including peptide yield and competition from COS hydrolysis.
Verify threonine formation using characterized glycylglycine as the substrate rather than transferring an unspecified oligoglycine result.
Measure free versus peptide-bound threonine and demonstrate compatible processing between coupling and hydrolytic release.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Historical HCN/ammonia studies support threonine detection after hydrolysis of complex products. Representing this as an unresolved multistage ensemble, without inventing a polymer molecular identity, is appropriate. Nevertheless, the provisional equation does not establish carbon allocation, coproduct yields or productive flux. Concentrated HCN processing followed by strong analytical hydrolysis establishes laboratory access to a hydrolyzable precursor pool, not demonstrated accumulation of free threonine in the stated surface environment. The network acknowledges this distinction but does not resolve it.
suggestions: Attach the specific historical experiment and report cyanide concentration, reaction duration, hydrolysis conditions and threonine yield.
Keep precursor generation and analytical hydrolysis separately annotated within the ensemble, without assigning a fictitious residue formula.
Supply a physically justified concentration mechanism and test release of free threonine under environmental conditions.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Sweeney et al. and Draganic et al. support threonine recovery from hydrolyzed irradiated cyanide solutions, making the laboratory ensemble credible. The unresolved radical/oligomer chemistry is appropriately disclosed. The principal environmental gap is dosimetry: the reported laboratory dose rate of approximately 2 kGy/h cannot be assumed for a terrestrial surface setting. Neither a natural source and irradiation timescale nor environmentally effective hydrolysis is specified. Provisional CO2 and ammonia coefficients are not experimentally established product distributions.
suggestions: Specify a natural radiation source, absorbed dose rate, cumulative dose and exposure time.
Compare precursor formation with radiolytic destruction and chemical loss over that exposure.
Distinguish post-irradiation analytical recovery from free-threonine formation under a tested environmental hydrolysis regime.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Parker et al. provide direct threonine detection from the relevant H2S-rich discharge configuration. An ensemble representation is warranted because the detailed target-forming mechanism was not resolved. The main uncertainty is environmental implementation: the strongly reducing gas mixture, gas-water cycling, discharge exposure and possible electrode/sulfur effects are not specified for the proposed surface setting. The balanced equation is a formal output constraint rather than a measured conversion of the gas mixture exclusively into threonine, hydrogen and sulfur.
suggestions: Define a local or transient setting capable of sustaining the required gas composition, pressure, water contact and discharge exposure.
Assess whether threonine production persists without the experimental tungsten-electrode configuration.
Report absolute target recovery, workup conditions and competing products instead of interpreting the balance closure as a yield model.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The supplied Matthews-Moser literature supports threonine recovery after hydrolysis of residues from dry methane/ammonia discharge chemistry. Including water in the overall equation is not contradictory because hydrolysis is explicitly subsequent to the dry stage. However, environmental maintenance of the dry reducing gas mixture, residue preservation and subsequent hydrolysis remain unquantified. The ensemble is a defensible representation of laboratory accessibility, but not yet a demonstrated route to environmentally accumulated free threonine.
suggestions: Specify dry-stage gas composition, pressure, discharge energy and duration, followed by separate wet-stage hydrolysis conditions.
Provide a physical scenario for preserving and wetting the discharge residue without assuming immediate quantitative amino-acid release.
Attach the original analytical evidence and distinguish measured threonine recovery from provisional hydrogen and carbon allocations.

evaluation.network_feedback: The network is structurally strong: all 27 molecule nodes and 20 reaction nodes belong to a connected graph, and molecule identifiers are used consistently. Under the stipulated deterministic check, every reaction is balanced or balanceable; none is classified here as a conservation violation. The problematic-reaction lists identify chemical-evidence or environmental gaps instead. The network aligns substantially with the supplied literature and appropriately distinguishes demonstrated precursor chemistry, post-hydrolysis detections, implementation candidates and unresolved ensembles. P4 provides the strongest endpoint-supported backbone, while P1 and P5 offer complementary, credible routes. The principal limitations are operational: 'Surface' alone does not establish reaction-specific pH, temperature, concentration, catalyst availability, energy exposure or residence time. Reaction-level citations are also absent from the submitted records. Explicitly acknowledging strong laboratory hydrolysis and speculative environmental extensions is scientifically appropriate, but does not demonstrate those steps in nature. Integrated precursor survival, competing reactions and free-threonine accumulation remain unquantified. Provisional ensemble coefficients and stereoisomer balance coefficients must not be interpreted as measured yields or product ratios. Racemic threonine can contain the L-threonine target; lack of enantiopurity is not treated as failure to produce it. Overall, this is a credible research network, but it does not meet the 0.9 network-approval threshold. Pathway approval flags use the separately requested 0.8 threshold.
